lesson.title: Automatic Repeat Request: Manufacturing Reliability Out of an Unreliable Channel
lesson.summary: Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ) is the family of error-control techniques that combine error detection, acknowledgments, and retransmission timers so that a link with a nonzero bit error rate can still deliver data reliably to the layer above it.
lesson.body:
Every physical link has some bit error rate: electrical noise, interference, and attenuation flip bits or destroy frames outright. Yet applications above the data link and transport layers expect reliable delivery, meaning every byte arrives, arrives once, and arrives in order. Automatic Repeat reQuest is the general strategy for closing that gap. Rather than trying to eliminate errors at the physical layer, which is expensive and never perfect, ARQ accepts that some frames will be lost or corrupted and builds a feedback loop that detects the damage and repairs it by resending data.

Every ARQ scheme rests on the same four pieces of machinery. First, an error-detecting code, typically a checksum or a cyclic redundancy check, is attached to each frame so the receiver can tell a corrupted frame from a good one. Second, the receiver sends acknowledgments back to the sender for frames it accepted correctly. Third, the sender keeps a copy of every unacknowledged frame in a retransmission buffer and starts a timer when it sends it. Fourth, if the timer expires before an acknowledgment arrives, the sender assumes the frame, or its acknowledgment, was lost and retransmits automatically, with no human or upper layer intervention needed, hence the name.

Sequence numbers are the detail that makes this reliable rather than merely hopeful. Without them, a receiver cannot tell a genuinely new frame from a retransmission of one it already accepted, and a sender cannot match an incoming acknowledgment to the frame it acknowledges. A single bit of sequence number is enough for the simplest scheme, alternating between 0 and 1 on successive frames. Richer schemes use wider fields to allow many frames in flight at once.

Consider a concrete trace. The sender transmits frame 0. Line noise flips several bits in transit, and the receiver's CRC check fails, so it silently discards the frame and sends nothing back. The sender's timer for frame 0 expires after time T with no acknowledgment received, so it retransmits frame 0. This time the frame arrives intact, the receiver returns ACK0, and the sender advances to send frame 1. That one retransmission, triggered purely by a timeout rather than an explicit error report, is the essence of ARQ: the absence of an acknowledgment is itself treated as evidence of failure.

ARQ is a general contract, not a single protocol, and the concepts that follow it, stop and wait, go back N, and selective repeat, are specific policies for how many frames a sender is allowed to have outstanding at once and how the receiver organizes its acknowledgments. The right choice depends heavily on the bit error rate of the underlying link and its bandwidth delay product. A very reliable link can tolerate an aggressive policy that keeps many frames in flight, while a noisy or long delay link needs to weigh the cost of retransmitting large batches of data against the throughput gained by not stopping after every single frame.
